entries.title: Keep cloud-delivered protection on (MAPS membership Advanced)
entries.rationale: Cloud-delivered protection is the lookup that lets Defender judge a file it has never seen. Block at first seen, the cloud block level and several attack surface reduction rules depend on it: Microsoft states that some rules 'must enable cloud-delivered protection' and that the cloud protection level can only be configured after cloud protection is on. This is the one place where the tool deliberately keeps a data flow to Microsoft switched on, because the protection that depends on it is worth more than the privacy it costs; automatic sample upload is a separate, manual choice (def-028).
entries.impact: Defender sends file and URL metadata for files it cannot judge locally to Microsoft's cloud service. On a default Windows 11 Home install the setting is normally already on, so the entry usually changes nothing; it restores the setting when a tweak tool or an earlier change switched it off.

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Set-MpPreference (read 2026-11-15)
evidence.claim: MAPSReporting: "Specifies the type of membership in Microsoft Active Protection Service." The accepted values are Disabled (0), Basic (1) and Advanced (2); the value 2 is written here.

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Specify the cloud protection level (read 2026-11-15)

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Attack surface reduction rules reference (read 2026-11-15)
evidence.claim: For the rules 'Block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion', 'Block execution of potentially obfuscated scripts' and 'Use advanced protection against ransomware': "To use this ASR rule, you must enable cloud-delivered protection."

entries.title: Keep real-time protection switched on (Defender never disabled)
entries.rationale: Hardening only: this entry makes sure real-time protection (scanning of files when they are opened or run) is on and never turns anything off. Tweak tools and malware both switch these Defender layers off; writing DisableRealtimeMonitoring = False puts the layer back. Defender itself stays the antivirus of the system, as the project's never-touch list requires.
entries.impact: No change on a system where real-time protection is already on (the Windows default). Where it was switched off, it is switched on again, with the usual cost of on-access scanning.

entries.title: Block potentially unwanted applications (adware, bundlers)
entries.rationale: Potentially unwanted applications are the adware, bundled installers and similar software that this tool's whole purpose is to keep off the system. With PUA protection on, Defender blocks them when they are downloaded, moved, run or installed and quarantines them. The setting is a Defender preference, so it needs no policy engine that Home lacks.
entries.impact: Installers that bundle optional extras, some download managers and cracked or key-generator tools can be blocked and quarantined. Defender shows a notification prefaced with 'PUA:'. The release is done in Windows Security under Protection history.

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Detect and block potentially unwanted applications (read 2026-11-15)
evidence.claim: "Microsoft Defender Antivirus blocks detected PUA files and any attempts to download, move, run, or install them." "Blocked PUA files are then moved to quarantine." The command is `Set-MpPreference -PUAProtection Enabled`; the documented values are 0 (off), 1 (on, detected items are blocked) and 2 (audit mode). The categories include "Advertising software that displays advertisements or promotions".

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Set-MpPreference (read 2026-11-15)

entries.title: Raise the cloud block level to High
entries.rationale: A higher cloud block level makes Defender block unknown files more aggressively while it waits for the cloud verdict. Level High is the first step above Default. Zero tolerance ('Blocks all unknown executable files') is deliberately not allowed by the policy file because it would block every new program on a general-purpose PC; High plus is not used because Microsoft says it might affect client performance. Entry def-001 (cloud protection) must be on first.
entries.impact: Microsoft states that this level 'increases the chance of false positives': a rarely seen, harmless program can be blocked for a short time or quarantined. It also makes the notification pop-up of the rule 'Block executable content from email client and webmail' appear (def-015), which at the default level blocks silently.

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Specify the cloud protection level (read 2026-11-15)
evidence.claim: High: "Aggressively blocks unknown files while optimizing client performance. This option increases the chance of false positives." Zero tolerance: "Blocks all unknown executable files." The command is `Set-MpPreference -CloudBlockLevel High`; the valid values are Default, High, HighPlus and ZeroTolerance. "Turn on cloud protection before you configure the cloud protection level."

entries.title: Turn on network protection in block mode
entries.rationale: Network protection extends Defender's SmartScreen-style reputation checks from the browser to every program: connections to malicious or suspicious domains are blocked at the network layer, which also covers malware that never opens a browser. The page read lists Windows 11 Pro and Enterprise only, so on Home the setting is written as 'inert if ignored' and the entry is marked unverified until a Home VM shows that it acts.
entries.impact: Programs lose connections to sites that Defender's reputation service flags; legitimate but flagged sites are blocked too. Microsoft recommends audit mode first ('use audit mode in a test environment to identify apps that would be blocked'); this tool does not ship an audit-mode entry because audit mode is not a hardening. Requires Defender in active mode with real-time protection on.

entries.title: Turn on controlled folder access (ransomware protection)
entries.rationale: Controlled folder access lets only trusted programs write to the protected folders (Documents, Pictures and similar), which stops ransomware from encrypting them. It is the strongest anti-ransomware control Defender offers, and it is the reason this entry exists at profile 3 despite its cost in convenience.
entries.impact: Programs that Defender does not trust can no longer change files in the protected folders: installers, games that save to Documents, photo and video editors, backup tools and scripts will fail with an access error until the program is allowed in Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Ransomware protection > Allow an app through Controlled folder access. Exclude this entry from the plan when that is not acceptable.

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Enable controlled folder access (read 2026-11-15)
evidence.claim: The command is `Set-MpPreference -EnableControlledFolderAccess <Mode>`; the modes are 0 or Disabled (default), 1 or Enabled, 2 or AuditMode, 3 or BlockDiskModificationOnly, 4 or AuditDiskModificationOnly. "The Windows Security app supports only On (equivalent to the Enabled mode) and Off (the Disabled mode)." "After you assess the effect of CFA in Audit Mode, you can set it to Enabled."

entries.title: Attest that Defender tamper protection is on
entries.rationale: Tamper protection stops other software from switching Defender's own settings off, including through the registry. It cannot be changed by this tool or by any script (Microsoft says changes made through a management tool 'might appear to succeed, but tamper protection blocks the changes'), so the tool only reports whether it is on. A failing check means 'tamper protection not attested', never a silent pass.
entries.impact: Read-only. Prints one line in the report and changes nothing.

audit.manual_check: Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Virus & threat protection settings > Tamper Protection reads On.

"Attempts to modify Microsoft Defender Antivirus settings through the registry are blocked." "When tamper protection is turned on, changes made through a management tool, including Group Policy, might appear to succeed, but tamper protection blocks the changes." "To check both settings, see Determine the status of tamper protection and real-time protection using PowerShell."

evidence.claim: The property name IsTamperProtected of Get-MpComputerStatus comes from general knowledge of the Defender module: it is not in the pages read (the MSFT_MpComputerStatus class page lists RealTimeProtectionEnabled, AntivirusEnabled, BehaviorMonitorEnabled, IoavProtectionEnabled and NISEnabled, and no tamper property). entries.title: ASR rule, block mode: block abuse of exploited vulnerable signed drivers
entries.rationale: Stops programs from loading signed drivers that are known to be vulnerable and exploited, a route malware uses to get into the kernel and switch protection off. It is one of Microsoft's three standard protection rules and works at the antivirus level, independent of the Windows vulnerable driver blocklist.
entries.impact: A driver on Microsoft's exploited list fails to load; very old hardware drivers may be affected. Typical systems notice nothing.

entries.title: ASR rule, block mode: block untrusted and unsigned processes that run from USB
entries.rationale: Prevents unsigned or untrusted executable files from running from USB drives and SD cards, which stops malware that spreads on removable media.
entries.impact: Portable programs that are not signed cannot be started from a USB drive. Copying them to the disk first does not help: the rule blocks the copy when it runs.

entries.title: ASR rule, block mode: block process creations originating from PSExec and WMI commands
entries.rationale: Blocks processes that are started remotely through PsExec or WMI, the way attackers move from one computer to another.
entries.impact: Remote administration tools that use PsExec or WMI to start programs (and some software deployment tools) fail. A home PC rarely uses either. Microsoft warns not to use other deployment methods for this rule on devices managed by Configuration Manager.

entries.title: ASR rule, warn mode: block executable files from running unless they meet a prevalence, age, or trusted list criterion
entries.rationale: Blocks executable files that are new, rare or untrusted until Defender's cloud has judged them. It is the strictest rule of the set, so it is set to Warn, not Block: the user sees a notification and can allow a program once. The rule relies on cloud-delivered protection (def-001).
entries.impact: New or rarely used programs trigger a warning the first time they run; users select Unblock to continue for 24 hours. Expect warnings after every software installation.

entries.title: Decide about automatic sample submission (manual choice, not changed by the tool)
entries.rationale: Automatic sample submission is the one Defender data flow that this tool does not change. Its default sends 'safe' samples (files unlikely to hold personal data) to Microsoft automatically; the alternatives are to be asked every time or never to send. Block at first seen holds a new file back until the cloud has judged it, and that judgment can need the file: switching submission off therefore weakens a protection layer, which the project's rule 'hardening only' does not allow the tool to do on its own. The choice is the user's.
entries.impact: Nothing is changed by the tool. The report prints the manual steps.
manual_steps: Open Windows Security > Virus & threat protection > Virus & threat protection settings > Manage settings.

Find 'Automatic sample submission'. Leave it On to keep block at first seen at full strength; switch it Off if you prefer that no file leaves the PC without being asked, and accept that Defender then judges new files with less help from the cloud.

audit.manual_check: Windows Security > Virus & threat protection settings > Manage settings > Automatic sample submission shows the state you chose. The setting is SubmitSamplesConsent in Get-MpPreference: 0 always prompt, 1 send safe samples (default), 2 never send, 3 send all samples.

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Set-MpPreference (read 2026-11-15)
evidence.claim: SubmitSamplesConsent: "Specifies how Windows Defender checks for user consent for certain samples." "If consent has previously been granted, Windows Defender submits the samples. Otherwise, if the MAPSReporting parameter does not have a value of Disabled, Windows Defender prompts the user for consent." The values are 0 Always prompt, 1 Send safe samples automatically, 2 Never send, 3 Send all samples automatically.

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Set-MpPreference (read 2026-11-15)
evidence.claim: DisableBlockAtFirstSeen: "Indicates whether to enable block at first seen."

evidence.source: learn.microsoft.com Set-MpPreference (read 2026-11-15)
evidence.claim: That block at first seen can need the file itself is general knowledge about how the feature works and is not stated in the pages read; it is the reason the entry is a manual choice.
